stories.title: Shenzhen summit yields declaration, but no Ukraine breakthrough
body: The leaders of the US, China and Russia met on 19 November and issued a broad declaration on nuclear risk and international cooperation. The joint statement did not establish a new arms-control framework or resolve the Ukraine war. The distinction between summit diplomacy and enforceable agreements matters particularly to governments absent from the talks.

stories.title: European allies seek assurances after US-Russia-China talks
body: US envoy Jared Kushner said he believed Moscow could accept NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine, but that assessment was not a signed Russian undertaking. US officials briefed European allies after the summit; no peace settlement was announced.

stories.title: International court's Rohingya genocide ruling raises the question of enforcement
body: The International Court of Justice ruled on 19 November that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during the military campaign of 2017. Myanmar rejected the judgment. The ruling is a landmark determination of state responsibility, but it is not itself a mechanism for safely repatriating refugees or ending the fighting inside Myanmar.

Roughly 1.2 million Rohingya are living in Bangladesh, according to Reuters reporting from Cox's Bazar. Refugees welcomed the ruling while confronting the absence of secure conditions for return. Bangladesh wants repatriation, but a credible path would require safety, rights, monitoring and meaningful political change inside Myanmar. The distinction between legal accountability and implementation is central to the story.

stories.title: COP31 negotiations run past deadline as fossil-fuel dispute persists
body: Climate negotiators in Antalya were set to continue beyond Friday's scheduled conclusion after a draft agreement omitted explicit fossil-fuel transition language. Delegates also disagreed over adaptation finance, with a proposed quantified $120 billion annual target absent from the latest text.

This was a negotiating draft, not a final adopted agreement. Countries dependent on fossil-fuel revenues, vulnerable states demanding finance and governments seeking faster decarbonisation entered the final phase with different priorities. The ultimate measure of success will be what countries formally adopt and how they implement it.

stories.title: EU industrial policy puts Britain's China-EV strategy under strain
body: Proposed European-content requirements for subsidies and procurement could exclude UK-made vehicles and components. Britain wants preferential access, but alignment could require a tougher position on Chinese EV imports, creating a trade-off between industrial integration and affordable electric cars. Negotiations have not produced a deal.

stories.title: Tulip Siddiq considers legal action over Bangladesh conviction
body: Former UK minister Tulip Siddiq says she may sue Bangladesh's former interim leader Muhammad Yunus after a conviction in absentia. She denies wrongdoing and disputes the fairness of the proceedings. The reported intention to sue is not an action already filed or a judicial finding in her favour.

stories.title: Britain and EU seal food-trade and youth-mobility reset
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders agreed on 20 November to ease trade in animals and plant products, establish youth mobility arrangements and link emissions-trading systems. The package represents a tangible post-Brexit rapprochement, although most changes will not take effect immediately.

Britain estimates that streamlined food trade could add £5.1 billion annually to its economy; this is a government projection, not an observed benefit. The carbon-market link is planned from 2028. Negotiators deferred the dispute over tuition fees for EU students at British universities and left the larger question of Britain's future alignment with EU rules unresolved.

stories.title: University fees remain an obstacle despite the UK–EU summit breakthrough
body: Britain and the European Union postponed agreement on tuition fees for students crossing the Channel. EU governments want their students to pay domestic rates at British universities, while London has preferred a less sweeping reduction. The sides set a further six-month negotiating period.

The disagreement is financially material to universities that rely on international-fee income and to families weighing the cost of study abroad. It illustrates the limits of the summit's reset: mobility and trade agreements can progress while politically sensitive questions about access to public institutions remain unsettled.

stories.title: British carmakers face unresolved EU industrial-policy trade-off
body: At the UK–EU summit, access for British-made cars to European-content subsidy and procurement rules remained bound up with questions about alignment on Chinese vehicle imports. Brussels has sought protections against third-country circumvention; London has been reluctant to mirror every EU trade restriction.

This is not a completed arrangement granting British cars preferential treatment. For manufacturers with integrated cross-Channel supply chains, the eventual rules could influence investment decisions and production locations. Consumers and importers would also be affected if alignment made lower-cost Chinese electric vehicles harder to obtain.

stories.title: White House seeks to shield officials from ABA depositions
body: The administration asked a federal court to block questioning of senior officials in the American Bar Association's lawsuit challenging executive orders targeting law firms. The ABA alleges retaliation for protected legal work and speech; the administration rejects that account and cites executive privilege. The court has not resolved the requested depositions.

stories.title: Federal court finds USDA religious emails unconstitutional
body: A federal judge ruled that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins' Christian messages to staff violated the First Amendment, according to AP's 19 November account. This is a judicial ruling on government communications, not a general prohibition on individual employees' religious expression.

stories.title: Congress confronts December funding deadline amid Iran-war dispute
body: Federal government funding expires on 11 December, and lawmakers are struggling to reach a deal over appropriations and the cost of the war involving Iran. President Donald Trump has sought an additional $350 billion for the Pentagon; senators are debating a defence bill that includes only part of that request.

A shutdown is a risk, not a fact. Democrats disagree over whether a funding confrontation can meaningfully restrain military operations, while Republicans have not settled on whether to pursue a party-line budget procedure. Congress must decide how to fund agencies during the transition to a new congressional majority after the midterm elections.

stories.title: Senate rejection of Iran war-powers measure sharpens oversight dispute
body: Senate Republicans voted on 19 November against a measure directing the president to end the Iran war or seek congressional authorisation to continue. The vote came amid public concern about the conflict and debate over the constitutional allocation of war powers.

The measure's defeat does not itself settle the constitutional argument. The executive and Congress retain competing instruments over military action and spending, and the funding deadline gives the dispute an immediate institutional dimension. Reporting must distinguish a vote on war powers from an actual withdrawal of appropriated military funds.

stories.title: Bangladesh-linked legal dispute crosses into British politics
body: The case involving former minister Tulip Siddiq illustrates the cross-border political consequences of Bangladesh's post-Hasina accountability proceedings. Siddiq disputes the case and says she was convicted without adequate notice. This desk does not independently establish the merits of the underlying corruption allegation.

stories.title: Nepal's prime minister prepares India visit after catastrophic floods
body: Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to meet Narendra Modi during a two-day India visit beginning Monday. The trip follows destructive August floods that killed about 1,500 people and left thousands missing, according to Reuters, and it will focus in part on reconstruction assistance.

Trade, energy infrastructure and transport links are also on the agenda. Nepal seeks additional air connectivity, while India is a leading trading partner and donor. The meeting is prospective: any new financing or infrastructure commitments should be reported only after formal announcement, with promised assistance separated from money actually disbursed.

stories.title: Rohingya refugees welcome genocide judgment but face prolonged displacement
body: Rohingya families in Bangladesh welcomed the International Court of Justice's finding that Myanmar committed genocide in 2017. Their celebrations, reported from Cox's Bazar, coexist with deep uncertainty about whether they will ever be able to return home safely.

Bangladesh faces pressure from the cost of hosting approximately 1.2 million refugees while international assistance is strained. Myanmar's continuing conflict makes repatriation a humanitarian and security challenge even after the judgment. This South Asia account centres the refugees and Bangladesh's responsibilities, rather than repeating the World desk's legal analysis.

stories.title: India's role in COP31 electrification dispute
body: The Antalya draft retained an aspirational goal for electricity to account for 35% of final energy use by 2035, but loosened language on national obligations and low-carbon supply. Reporting identified India among countries resisting stronger wording. The document remained a negotiating draft, not adopted Indian policy.

stories.title: Delimitation debate exposes differences among Maharashtra opposition parties
body: Maharashtra political reporting on 19 November described disagreement within the opposition alliance after Supriya Sule indicated conditional support for changes to a constituency-redrawing bill. The reported stance is conditional and should not be treated as a final legislative vote or an agreed alliance position.

stories.title: Voter-roll deletions draw US rights criticism and Indian rebuttal
body: A US government religious-freedom commission accused India of discriminating against Muslim citizens in a nationwide electoral-roll revision. Reuters reported that approximately 130 million entries were removed. India's Election Commission says the exercise targets deceased, duplicate, relocated and otherwise ineligible voters and provides appeal mechanisms.

Deletion from a voter list is not proof of foreign nationality. The US commission's recommendations are nonbinding; India's foreign ministry rejected the criticism as politically biased. The most important unresolved questions are how many eligible citizens were wrongly excluded, whether appeals are effective and whether electoral-roll processes have been improperly connected to immigration enforcement.

stories.title: Wheat planting faces possible sharp decline as farmers change crops
body: Industry estimates suggest Indian wheat acreage could decline by roughly 6% as drought and changing crop economics affect planting decisions. The estimate is a projection during the sowing season, not a completed agricultural census.

A sustained acreage fall could complicate grain procurement, food-price management and farmers' income expectations. Weather, irrigation access and government purchase prices will determine the eventual harvest more than one early forecast. The edition will not convert this preliminary estimate into a confirmed production shortfall.

stories.title: Electoral-roll exclusions raise questions beyond administrative accuracy
body: A Reuters investigation documented families facing detention, deportation or citizenship questioning after names disappeared from electoral rolls. The reporting included West Bengal, where Muslim voters accounted for a disproportionate share of certain deletions. The Election Commission and the government maintain that the revision is an eligibility exercise.

The legal and democratic distinction is fundamental: being absent from a voter register does not establish a person's nationality. Cases under judicial challenge, individual testimonies, official statistics and government denials must be evaluated separately. The story's significance lies in due process and the ability of citizens to restore their electoral rights.

stories.title: Versova residents protest coastal-road tree removal
body: Residents organised a Chipko-style protest at Nana Nani Park after tree-felling began for the Versova-Bhayandar Coastal Road. Reporting says 184 trees are slated for removal and another 164 for transplantation. The dispute highlights the local environmental costs of transport expansion; the figures are project-reported, not a verified count of trees already felled.

stories.title: BMC begins Bhendi Bazaar building demolition amid police deployment
body: Mumbai's municipal corporation began demolishing the dilapidated Musafirkhana building on 19 November, after local objections delayed the work. The building has historical associations with D Company, but the current civic action was reported as demolition for safety and redevelopment.

stories.title: Maharashtra prioritises drinking water as drought affects most talukas
body: Maharashtra authorities have identified 310 of 358 talukas as drought-affected and directed officials to defer non-essential new construction spending to prioritise drinking-water supply and mitigation, according to 20 November reporting. The scale of the designation makes this a statewide public-services and fiscal story.

The practical test is whether district administrations can deliver reliable water, protect livelihoods and fund urgent work before conditions worsen. A drought designation does not mean every community faces identical shortages. Local reservoir levels, tanker deployment, agricultural losses and the state order itself need continuing scrutiny.

stories.title: Mumbai and Thane air quality renews focus on pollution enforcement
body: Air-quality readings reported on 20 November indicated unhealthy conditions across parts of Mumbai and neighbouring Thane. Construction dust, traffic and industrial emissions are recurring concerns, but a single citywide index cannot identify the precise source of pollution.

Readers need the station, timestamp and Indian AQI methodology before interpreting a reported number. Public accountability extends to dust-control inspections, roadworks, waste burning and the health implications for children, outdoor workers and people with respiratory conditions. This is a local environmental-health issue rather than merely a weather update.

stories.title: Streaming release brings FTX story to scripted television
body: The Altruists, a dramatisation of the FTX collapse starring Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle, was listed for a 19 November streaming release. The adaptation raises the familiar distinction between dramatised narrative and the documented record of the exchange's failure.

stories.title: Grand Theft Auto VI arrives to exceptional reviews and industry-scale expectations
body: Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI began its worldwide rollout on 19 November after years of anticipation. Early critical reviews were exceptionally strong, with the game returning to the fictional Vice City and placing a central relationship between its two protagonists at the heart of the story.

The commercial significance reaches beyond a single release: developers, publishers and platform operators will be watching sales and player engagement. Early review scores and analyst sales forecasts are not final audited sales results. The game's vast production ambitions also raise questions about development costs, working conditions and the sustainability of blockbuster budgets.

stories.title: Critics debate GTA VI's storytelling as well as technical spectacle
body: Reviews of Grand Theft Auto VI have praised the detail of its open world, but some critics have placed unusual emphasis on the emotional relationship between Lucia and Jason. The response suggests that the game is being assessed not only as a technical achievement but also as a work of narrative popular culture.

Review aggregation is a snapshot of critical reception, not a representative poll of players or proof of enduring artistic standing. The cultural question is whether an enormously expensive franchise can offer meaningful storytelling while retaining the satire, violence and player freedom associated with its predecessors.

stories.title: Ramayana box-office figures underline pan-India reach
body: Industry tracking cited in 19 November coverage placed Ramayana's domestic net box office around ₹844 crore after its fourteenth day, with especially strong reported performance in Kerala. These are trade estimates, not independently audited final distributor receipts; net, gross and worldwide totals should not be mixed.

stories.title: Ramayana enters third week with extraordinary receipts and slowing daily sales
body: Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana: Part 1 has reached a reported worldwide gross of about ₹1,547 crore after its fifteenth day, according to figures cited by The Indian Express. Its Thursday India net collection was estimated at ₹19.35 crore, down from the previous day, demonstrating that a major cumulative total can coexist with a slowing daily run.

Box-office reporting requires care: India net, India gross, overseas gross and worldwide gross are different measures, and early trade estimates can be revised. The film's multilingual distribution and scale are commercially consequential, but these figures should not be confused with the producers' profit or a verified return on production expenditure.

stories.title: Regional-language streaming slate spans Tamil and Telugu cinema
body: Release listings for Friday include the Tamil romantic thriller Anbil Avan on SonyLIV, the Telugu comedy thriller Anumana Pakshi on Sun NXT and the Telugu family comedy Crazy Kalyanam on Aha. The range illustrates how Indian screen culture cannot be reduced to Hindi theatrical releases.

These are platform release listings, not verified audience totals or reviews. Availability can differ by region and can change, so viewers should check the streaming service directly. For the industry, language-specific platforms and licensing strategies remain important alongside national theatrical blockbusters.

stories.title: Independent filmmaker questions studios' response to a smaller film's success
body: The director of Hanuman Ansh publicly questioned the lack of engagement from major studios after the film's reported success, according to The Indian Express. The comments bring attention to the uneven distribution of visibility, financing and marketing resources in Indian cinema.

A filmmaker's account of the industry's response is a perspective, not independent proof that particular studios deliberately withheld support. The broader structural question is how independent films obtain distribution and follow-on investment when attention is concentrated on large, star-led productions.

stories.title: India–New Zealand Test series opens in Wellington
body: The first Test was scheduled to begin on 19 November in Wellington, with the two-match series running into the following week. This is a fixture note rather than a verified live score; no result is asserted.

stories.title: Women's Asian Champions Trophy begins in Bhopal
body: The six-team women's hockey tournament was scheduled to begin on 19 November, with India facing Malaysia on opening day. The competition also features China, Japan, South Korea and Thailand. No unverified match outcome is reported.

stories.title: Jaiswal and Rahul lead India's response after New Zealand post 368
body: At stumps on day two of the first Test in Wellington, India were 159 for one in reply to New Zealand's 368. Yashasvi Jaiswal made 85 from 89 deliveries and KL Rahul remained unbeaten on 52. Henry Nicholls finished 175 not out for the hosts, while Glenn Phillips made 118.

India still trailed by 209 runs at the close, so the match remained open. Jasprit Bumrah took four wickets for 92, while the Nicholls–Phillips partnership had earlier rescued New Zealand. The score is explicitly a day-two position, not a final result; the second Test is scheduled for Christchurch next week.

stories.title: Football's Baller League announces global tournament for 2027
body: Organisers of the Baller League announced plans on 19 November to launch an international competition in 2027. The development reflects the spread of short-format, entertainment-oriented football products designed for digital audiences.

The announcement concerns a future tournament, not a completed competition or established commercial success. Its longer-term significance depends on confirmed teams, players, broadcast arrangements and governing-body relationships, and on whether novelty formats complement or compete with conventional football.

stories.title: Anthropic's Nasdaq debut tests AI valuations
body: Anthropic's shares opened above their $83 IPO price and closed at $97.17 on 19 November, a 17% gain, after a share sale exceeding $81 billion. The company's vast compute commitments and continuing losses mean a strong first session is not evidence of durable profitability.

stories.title: European shares slide as investors reassess technology risk
body: The STOXX 600 closed down 0.88% at 638.41 on 19 November, a fourth consecutive decline, as technology-sector valuations and weaker defensive sectors weighed on markets. One session's performance does not establish a sustained economic downturn.

stories.title: British blue chips fall to six-week low
body: The FTSE 100 ended Thursday down 0.9% at 10,452.68, while the FTSE 250 lost 0.7%. The moves occurred amid broader investor risk aversion; they are market closes, not forecasts for Friday.

stories.title: Global AI selloff sends Asian equities to their worst week since 2020
body: Global technology shares came under renewed pressure on Friday even after Anthropic's historic stock-market debut. Reuters reported the MSCI Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan was down about 8% for the week, its sharpest weekly decline since March 2020, while Taiwan's market fell even more steeply.

The immediate debate is whether immense AI infrastructure spending can translate into durable profits. Investors moved towards government bonds as equity volatility increased. These are market snapshots at the reporting cutoff; the economic question is broader than one company's IPO and includes financing costs, earnings expectations and concentration risk.

stories.title: Oil market balances Gulf shipping risk against surplus expectations
body: Oil prices were little changed on 19 November as disruptions linked to the Gulf conflict offset concern about excess global supply. Prices can therefore remain elevated relative to peacetime assumptions even when traders anticipate sufficient barrels in aggregate.

The effects reach beyond energy companies: shipping insurance, airline fuel, inflation and import bills are exposed to the risk of maritime disruption. A quoted price is a point-in-time market observation, not a forecast. Subsequent moves depend on actual shipping flows, production decisions and the conflict's trajectory.

stories.title: Indian equities rally against regional market weakness
body: The Nifty 50 rose 1.14% to 25,514.30 and the Sensex gained 1.21% to 83,021.75 on Thursday. Autos and banks led gains while IT declined; Reuters linked sentiment to lower commodity prices and renewed foreign inflows. The numbers are closing-market observations, not guarantees of further gains.

stories.title: RBI intervention recedes as capital returns
body: Reuters reported RBI net dollar sales including forward maturities of about $4.8 billion from 15 October to 6 November, versus $48 billion in the prior month. Stronger inflows and cheaper oil eased rupee pressure, but reserve and forward-book management remain important uncertainties.

stories.title: Airlines plan fewer domestic flights for November–December
body: An Indian Express analysis of Cirium schedules indicated 7,154 fewer domestic flights than the corresponding period last year, a 3.5% fall in scheduled flights. These are published schedules rather than verified flights operated, and may change with cancellations and revisions.

stories.title: India's foreign-exchange reserves drop $14.2 billion in one week
body: Reserve Bank of India data published Friday showed foreign-exchange reserves at $705.342 billion for the week ended 13 November, down from $719.547 billion a week earlier. Foreign-currency assets and gold holdings accounted for most of the reported decline.

The headline change should not be interpreted as an equivalent amount of spot-market intervention. Valuation shifts and foreign-exchange swap maturities also affect the dollar value of reserves. The rupee had weakened during the reference week but strengthened to about 92.67 per dollar on Friday, illustrating the importance of dates when comparing currency and reserve figures.

stories.title: SEBI consults on changes to governance of market infrastructure
body: India's securities regulator proposed changes to the tenure and age rules applying to leaders and independent directors of exchanges and other market infrastructure institutions. These bodies occupy a special position: they are commercial enterprises but also guardians of market integrity.

The proposals are part of a consultation process, not regulations already in force. The relevant trade-off is between continuity and expertise on one side and accountability, succession and conflicts of interest on the other. The final text and responses from exchanges will determine the practical effects.

stories.title: Regulator proposes easing enhanced foreign-investor disclosures
body: SEBI proposed removing additional disclosure obligations introduced in 2023 for certain foreign portfolio investors. The measure is intended to reduce compliance burdens but also raises questions about transparency into beneficial ownership and concentrated investments.

It remains a proposal, not a repeal. A proper assessment needs to identify which investors would be affected, what disclosure requirements would remain and whether the change would weaken the ability to detect opaque ownership structures. Market access and investor protection need not always be opposing objectives, but their balance requires evidence.

stories.title: Ocean alkalinity study finds mineral performance depends on dose
body: A September mesocosm study using northeastern Arabian Sea water found periclase increased alkalinity at modest dosing, while higher dosing triggered secondary precipitation and olivine dissolved slowly. It is experimental evidence about chemistry, not proof of atmospheric carbon removal at commercial scale.

stories.title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth after 49 years
body: NASA announced that Voyager 1 reached a distance of one light-day from Earth on 18 November. Light requires 24 hours to cross that distance, approximately 25.9 billion kilometres, meaning even a radio message from the spacecraft takes a day to arrive.

The achievement is a communications and engineering milestone rather than a sudden new scientific discovery. Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and continues to gather measurements beyond the heliosphere. Its ageing systems, limited power and very long signal delays make each successful scientific transmission remarkable.

stories.title: Medical-device researchers examine implications of EU AI regulation
body: A paper published in npj Digital Medicine examines proposed changes to European medical-device regulation and their consequences for AI-enabled devices. The subject is important because software that adapts or relies on data-driven models can pose validation and oversight challenges distinct from conventional equipment.

This is an analysis of regulatory proposals, not evidence that any particular AI medical product is safe or effective. Clinicians and regulators must still evaluate clinical performance, monitoring after deployment, transparency, and whether changes to algorithms require fresh assessment. The article is a policy analysis rather than a clinical trial.

stories.title: Anthropic IPO puts safety commitments under shareholder scrutiny
body: The newly listed AI developer faces pressure to balance expensive model training and investor expectations with its stated safeguards. Reuters described past clashes over military use and pauses to advanced-model training. These are reported company decisions and positions, not independent evidence that any model is safe.

stories.title: AI developers face lawsuit seeking restrictions on frontier-model work
body: A lawsuit filed against OpenAI, Google and Anthropic sought to halt frontier AI development, according to Reuters reporting earlier in November. The filing is part of a widening contest over how society should manage the risks of powerful systems before their capabilities and safeguards are fully understood.

A lawsuit's allegations are not judicial findings. The case raises difficult questions about standing, evidence of harm and the appropriate role of courts relative to legislatures and specialist regulators. It should be assessed separately from debates over competition, open research and the commercial viability of AI infrastructure.

stories.title: White House cyber coordinator's departure leaves policy questions
body: The White House's national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving his position, Reuters reported on 19 November. The office coordinates federal cybersecurity policy and strategy, making leadership continuity relevant to agencies and private operators of critical infrastructure.

A personnel departure alone is not evidence of a security breach or policy collapse. The substantive question is how the administration will maintain coordination across defence, civilian agencies and industry, particularly as cyber threats and AI-enabled security challenges evolve.

stories.title: COP31 draft drops explicit fossil-fuel transition language
body: The revised 19 November negotiating text removed fossil-fuel language and a proposed $120 billion adaptation-finance goal. It retained a weakened electrification ambition and a reference to carbon removal. Negotiators had not yet adopted the draft; the final outcome could differ.

stories.title: October's record global warmth remains the observational benchmark
body: Copernicus ERA5 estimated October 2026 global surface air temperature at 15.35°C, 0.90°C above 1991–2020 and 1.75°C above the estimated 1850–1900 baseline. This is a monthly reanalysis statistic published earlier in November, not a new 20 November measurement or proof that the Paris long-term threshold has formally been breached.

stories.title: Extra-polar ocean temperature sets October record
body: ERA5 estimates put mean sea-surface temperature across 60°S–60°N at 20.95°C for October, the fifth successive monthly record for its respective calendar month. Strong El Niño conditions contributed, but the figure is a global extra-polar average, not a local Indian Ocean measurement.

stories.title: COP31 carbon-removal wording draws scrutiny
body: The draft climate agreement encourages carbon-removal technologies without resolving how removal claims should be verified or how they relate to near-term fossil-fuel reductions. It is policy language, not evidence of tonnes removed; safeguards for additionality, permanence and ecological effects remain essential.

stories.title: Arabian Sea experiment warns against assuming all added minerals dissolve
body: A 2026 laboratory mesocosm study in northeastern Arabian Sea water found periclase dosing above roughly 1,000 micromoles per kilogram could induce secondary precipitation, while olivine dissolution was limited. The result matters for marine MRV and site selection; it is not a new field trial or independently verified carbon-credit delivery.

stories.title: UK–EU carbon-market link is agreed, but implementation comes later
body: Britain and the European Union agreed to link their emissions trading systems as part of their 20 November summit package. The link is scheduled from 2028 and could reduce the exposure of covered goods to each other's carbon-border levies.

The agreement does not itself remove emissions or establish an immediate unified carbon price. Implementation depends on market rules, technical compatibility and the treatment of carbon-border adjustments. Its importance lies in the interaction between industrial competitiveness and the integrity of emissions accounting.
